points: Peak power density reached 4.8 W per square metre of membrane area for the seawater draw solution, against 3.1 W per square metre for the river-water baseline, at draw and feed salinities of 35 g per litre and 0.5 g per litre.
Water flux averaged 18 L per square metre per hour at an applied hydraulic pressure of 12 bar on the draw side.
Reverse salt flux remained below 0.8 g per square metre per hour across the full test.
Power density held within five percent of the peak value over 30 days of continuous operation at a feed temperature of 20 °C.
The membrane support layer had a structural parameter of 450 µm, and the structural parameter sets the internal concentration polarisation loss.
No detectable change in power density was recorded across the feed pH range from six to eight, at fixed salinity and temperature.
definitions: PRO = pressure-retarded osmosis, a membrane process that converts a salinity difference into hydraulic pressure on the draw side
structural parameter = the product of support layer thickness and tortuosity divided by porosity, a length that measures resistance to solute diffusion in the support layer
limits: The stated power density applies to the flat-sheet configuration tested, and module-scale power density remains unmeasured.
figures: Fig. 1: power density and water flux over the full operating period
prose: Pressure-retarded osmosis (PRO) is a membrane process that converts a salinity difference into hydraulic pressure on the draw side, and PRO was operated here with a seawater draw solution against a river-water feed. Power density reached 4.8 W per square metre of membrane area for the seawater draw solution (3.1 W per square metre for the river-water baseline) at draw and feed salinities of 35 g per litre and 0.5 g per litre. Water flux averaged 18 L per square metre per hour at an applied hydraulic pressure of 12 bar on the draw side. Reverse salt flux remained below 0.8 g per square metre per hour across the full test, and the low reverse salt flux preserved the salinity gradient that drives the flux. Power density held within five percent of the peak value over 30 days of continuous operation at a feed temperature of 20 °C, with no cleaning cycle applied during the period. The membrane support layer had a structural parameter of 450 µm, the product of support layer thickness and tortuosity divided by porosity. The structural parameter sets the internal concentration polarisation loss, and the measured power density sits below the value the bulk salinity gradient alone would give. Fig. 1 shows power density and water flux over the full operating period, with the flux trace holding the same plateau as the power density trace. No detectable change in power density was recorded across the feed pH range from six to eight, at fixed salinity and temperature. The stated power density applies to the flat-sheet configuration tested, and module-scale power density remains unmeasured. Power density at module scale depends on flow distribution and pressure drop along the module, and neither quantity was measured in the flat-sheet cell. The salinity gradient is the energy source in the process, and the gradient was held by continuous draw and feed replacement throughout the test.

points: Slag viscosity fell from 0.62 Pa·s at a basicity of 0.9 to 0.28 Pa·s at a basicity of 1.3, measured at 1500 °C and a shear rate of 10 per second.
An alumina addition of 8 percent by mass raised slag viscosity to 0.51 Pa·s at the higher basicity.
Crystallisation began below 1420 °C, and the solid fraction at the onset point reached 15 percent by mass.
Viscosity values are reported for a cooling rate of 5 °C per minute, and faster cooling gave higher apparent viscosity in the same apparatus.
definitions: basicity = the mass ratio of calcium oxide to silicon dioxide in the slag
slag viscosity = the resistance of the molten slag to shear flow, reported in pascal seconds (Pa·s)
limits: The viscosity values hold for the synthetic slag compositions tested, and plant slags with iron oxide carry an added composition dependence that the synthetic series does not cover.
figures: Fig. 1: slag viscosity against basicity at the measurement temperature
prose: Basicity is the mass ratio of calcium oxide to silicon dioxide in the slag, and slag viscosity is the resistance of the molten slag to shear flow, reported in pascal seconds (Pa·s). Slag viscosity fell from 0.62 Pa·s at a basicity of 0.9 to 0.28 Pa·s at a basicity of 1.3, measured at 1500 °C and a shear rate of 10 per second. The fall in slag viscosity with basicity records the breakdown of the silicate network as calcium oxide supplies free oxygen to the melt. Fig. 1 shows slag viscosity against basicity at the measurement temperature, and the curve steepens in the same basicity interval where the network breakdown is strongest. An alumina addition of 8 percent by mass raised slag viscosity to 0.51 Pa·s at the higher basicity. Alumina enters the silicate network as a network former in calcium-rich melts, and the viscosity rise records that network role. Crystallisation began below 1420 °C, and the solid fraction at the onset point reached 15 percent by mass. Apparent viscosity rose sharply once crystals formed, and the reported fluid values end at the crystallisation onset. Each composition was melted and measured in three replicate melts, and the replicate spread stayed inside the interval set by the viscometer calibration. Viscosity values are reported for a cooling rate of 5 °C per minute, and faster cooling gave higher apparent viscosity in the same apparatus. The viscosity values hold for the synthetic slag compositions tested, and plant slags with iron oxide carry an added composition dependence that the synthetic series does not cover. Slag viscosity controls slag drainage and metal droplet settling in the furnace, and the basicity interval studied brackets the interval used in routine furnace operation.

points: Peak pile temperature reached 63 °C at the pile centre, and the pile held above 55 °C for 9 days during the thermophilic phase.
The thermophilic phase lasted 16 days from the start of the trial, against an ambient temperature of 14 °C over the same period.
The pile held 850 kg of mixed green and woody feedstock at a moisture content of 58 percent by mass and a carbon to nitrogen ratio of 28.
The pile was turned every 4 days, and oxygen concentration at the pile centre stayed above 11 percent by volume between turnings.
Indicator organism counts fell by 3 log units between the start of the trial and the end of the thermophilic phase.
definitions: thermophilic phase = the period of a composting run during which pile temperature stays in the range favoured by heat-tolerant microorganisms
log unit = a tenfold change in a count, used to report reductions in organism numbers
limits: The temperature profile holds for the windrow scale and feedstock mix tested, and smaller piles lose heat faster through the pile surface.
figures: Fig. 1: pile temperature at the centre and at the surface over the trial
prose: The thermophilic phase is the period of a composting run during which pile temperature stays in the range favoured by heat-tolerant microorganisms, and the phase structure governs the temperature profile reported here. Peak pile temperature reached 63 °C at the pile centre, and the pile held above 55 °C for 9 days during the thermophilic phase. The thermophilic phase lasted 16 days from the start of the trial, against an ambient temperature of 14 °C over the same period. Fig. 1 shows pile temperature at the centre and at the surface over the trial, and the surface trace peaks later and lower than the centre trace. The pile held 850 kg of mixed green and woody feedstock at a moisture content of 58 percent by mass and a carbon to nitrogen ratio of 28. The pile was turned every 4 days, and oxygen concentration at the pile centre stayed above 11 percent by volume between turnings. Turning restored the oxygen concentration within hours, and the temperature trace recovered the pre-turning value on the same day. Indicator organism counts fell by 3 log units between the start of the trial and the end of the thermophilic phase, a log unit being a tenfold change in a count. The count reduction tracks the period above the peak threshold, and the reduction rate slowed once the pile cooled into the curing range. Moisture loss during the thermophilic phase came mainly from the pile surface, and the centre stayed wet enough to sustain microbial activity throughout the phase. The temperature profile holds for the windrow scale and feedstock mix tested, and smaller piles lose heat faster through the pile surface. Temperature at the pile centre is the control variable for turning decisions in routine operation, and the profile gives the interval over which a single turning schedule held the phase.

points: The pressure drop problem has 7 physical variables and 3 fundamental dimensions, and the difference gives 4 dimensionless groups.
Worked example inputs: pipe diameter 0.1 m, mean velocity 2 m per second, fluid density 1000 kg per cubic metre, fluid viscosity 0.001 Pa·s, and a measured pressure drop of 850 Pa.
The Reynolds number for the worked example is 200000, computed from density, velocity, diameter and viscosity.
The Euler number for the worked example is 0.2125, computed from the pressure drop, the density and the velocity.
definitions: dimensionless group = a product of physical variables raised to powers chosen so that all units cancel
Reynolds number = the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces in a flow, formed from density, velocity, a length and viscosity
Euler number = the ratio of pressure forces to inertial forces, formed from a pressure difference, density and velocity
prose: This tutorial builds dimensionless groups for a pipe flow problem and checks each group before use. You start from a list of the physical variables that govern the problem, and the goal is a smaller set of dimensionless groups that carries the same physics. A dimensionless group is a product of physical variables raised to powers chosen so that all units cancel. The pressure drop problem has 7 physical variables and 3 fundamental dimensions, and the difference gives 4 dimensionless groups. Write the variable list with a unit for every variable, and count a variable once even where the variable appears in several parts of the apparatus. The worked example has three parts: the inputs, the group values, and a check on each group. Inputs for the worked example are a pipe diameter of 0.1 m, a mean velocity of 2 m per second, a fluid density of 1000 kg per cubic metre, a fluid viscosity of 0.001 Pa·s, and a measured pressure drop of 850 Pa. The Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces in a flow, formed from density, velocity, a length and viscosity. The Reynolds number for the worked example is 200000, computed from density, velocity, diameter and viscosity. A Reynolds number of this size places the example flow in the turbulent regime, and the regime tells you which friction correlations apply to the groups. The Euler number is the ratio of pressure forces to inertial forces, formed from a pressure difference, density and velocity. The Euler number for the worked example is 0.2125, computed from the pressure drop, the density and the velocity. Check each group by substituting the units of its variables and confirming that the units cancel in full; a group with a residual unit signals a wrong exponent. Record the groups with the input set that produced the groups, since a group value without its input set cannot be compared against a second experiment. Your own problems follow the same steps: list the variables, count the fundamental dimensions, form the groups, and check the units of each group before any group enters a correlation.

points: Worked example inputs: tank cross-sectional area 0.8 square metres, constant inflow 0.04 cubic metres per second, and an outflow coefficient of 0.02 cubic metres per second per metre of level.
The steady level for the worked example is 2 m, at which inflow and outflow are equal.
The time constant for the worked example is 40 s, from the cross-sectional area divided by the outflow coefficient.
The level starts at 0.5 m, and the initial departure from the steady level is 1.5 m.
At one time constant the departure factor is 0.368, and the level at one time constant is 1.448 m.
definitions: mass balance = an accounting equation that sets the rate of accumulation of a quantity inside a boundary equal to the rate in minus the rate out
time constant = the time over which a departure from a steady value falls by the factor stated for the exponential term
steady level = the liquid level at which inflow and outflow are equal and the level stops changing
prose: This tutorial writes an unsteady mass balance for a draining tank and solves the balance for the liquid level as a function of time. A mass balance is an accounting equation that sets the rate of accumulation of a quantity inside a boundary equal to the rate in minus the rate out. You write the accumulation term first, and the inflow and outflow terms follow from the streams crossing the tank boundary. The worked example has three parts: the inputs, the solution, and a check on the solution at its two ends. Inputs for the worked example are a tank cross-sectional area of 0.8 square metres, a constant inflow of 0.04 cubic metres per second, and an outflow coefficient of 0.02 cubic metres per second per metre of level. Outflow grows in proportion to the level under the stated coefficient, and the proportionality is the only level dependence in the balance. The steady level is the liquid level at which inflow and outflow are equal and the level stops changing. The steady level for the worked example is 2 m, at which inflow and outflow are equal. The time constant is the time over which a departure from a steady value falls by the factor stated for the exponential term. The time constant for the worked example is 40 s, from the cross-sectional area divided by the outflow coefficient. The level starts at 0.5 m, and the initial departure from the steady level is 1.5 m. At one time constant the departure factor is 0.368, and the level at one time constant is 1.448 m. Check the solution at the start point and at long time before use: the solution returns the starting level at zero time, and the solution approaches the steady level as time grows. A solution that misses either end point carries an error in the balance or in the algebra, and the error is cheaper to find at the check than in a design calculation. Your own tank problems follow the same steps: fix the boundary, write the accumulation term, and carry the units of every term through the balance.

points: The film emits at a peak wavelength of 630 nm with a full width at half maximum of 28 nm.
Photoluminescence quantum yield of the film reached 94 percent under blue excitation.
Colour gamut coverage reached 118 percent of the DCI-P3 standard at a film thickness of 12 µm.
Brightness retention was 91 percent after 1000 hours of operation at 85 °C.
definitions: quantum dot = a semiconductor crystal with a size of a few nanometres, whose emission wavelength is set by the crystal size
photoluminescence quantum yield = the fraction of absorbed photons that a material re-emits as light
FWHM = full width at half maximum, the width of an emission peak measured between the points at half of the peak height
prose: Display films based on quantum dots, semiconductor crystals with a size of a few nanometres whose emission wavelength is set by the crystal size, are assessed here as colour conversion layers for liquid crystal displays. The film was cast from a cadmium-free quantum dot dispersion in a polymer binder and cured under blue excitation. The film emits at a peak wavelength of 630 nm with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 28 nm, the FWHM being the width of an emission peak measured between the points at half of the peak height. Photoluminescence quantum yield of the film reached 94 percent under blue excitation, the quantum yield being the fraction of absorbed photons that the material re-emits as light. Colour gamut coverage reached 118 percent of the DCI-P3 standard at a film thickness of 12 µm. Brightness retention was 91 percent after 1000 hours of operation at 85 °C. The narrow emission width carries the gamut coverage, and the retention value places the film inside the operating envelope of a commercial backlight unit.

points: Nutrient solution in the reference system is held at an electrical conductivity between 1.2 and 1.8 mS per centimetre and a pH of 5.8.
Yield variation between bays in the reference facility reached 22 percent over a growth cycle of 28 days under a light period of 16 hours per day.
definitions: vertical farming = crop production in stacked layers inside a controlled indoor environment
electrical conductivity (EC) = a measure of the total dissolved salt concentration of a solution, reported in millisiemens per centimetre (mS per centimetre)
nutrient solution = the water-based solution that carries mineral nutrients to the crop roots
prose: Vertical farming is crop production in stacked layers inside a controlled indoor environment, and the nutrient solution is the water-based solution that carries mineral nutrients to the crop roots. Growing conditions inside a vertical farm are set by the operator: light, temperature, humidity and nutrient supply all sit under direct control, and crop response to a recipe change is measurable within a single growth cycle. Nutrient solution in the reference system is held at an electrical conductivity (EC) between 1.2 and 1.8 mS per centimetre and a pH of 5.8, EC being a measure of the total dissolved salt concentration of a solution, reported in millisiemens per centimetre. Recipe control at the tank is well established, and commercial systems hold EC and pH at the tank outlet within narrow bands. The distribution of the nutrient solution is less well characterised: concentration at the root zone differs from concentration at the tank outlet, and the difference varies with position in the rack. Yield variation between bays in the reference facility reached 22 percent over a growth cycle of 28 days under a light period of 16 hours per day, with light and temperature held uniform across the bays. The missing knowledge is the size and the cause of the root-zone concentration difference under production conditions. This study measures nutrient concentration at the root zone across a production rack, compares the root-zone values against the tank outlet values, and tests whether the bay yield pattern follows the concentration pattern. The measurements use in-line sensors at the tank outlet and sampled root-zone solution at matched times, on a leafy green crop grown under the reference recipe.

points: The array delivered 4.2 GWh over an 11 month trial, at an array capacity factor of 34 percent and an availability of 93 percent.
Wake loss at a downstream spacing of 5 rotor diameters held the downstream output deficit to 9 percent against the front-row value.
Capacity factor claims hold for sites with a peak spring current speed above 2.5 m per second; the trial site peak spring current speed was 3.1 m per second.
definitions: capacity factor = the ratio of the energy a turbine or array delivers over a period to the energy the turbine or array would deliver at rated power over the same period
availability = the fraction of a trial period during which a turbine stands ready to generate when the tidal current is sufficient
limits: The trial covers a single site and a single array layout, and array behaviour at a second site with a different seabed and a different current profile remains unmeasured.
Biofouling control during the trial used diver cleaning on a fixed schedule, and availability under a longer cleaning interval remains unmeasured.
prose: The trial supports a bounded claim about array performance at energetic tidal sites. Capacity factor is the ratio of the energy an array delivers over a period to the energy the array would deliver at rated power over the same period, and availability is the fraction of a trial period during which a turbine stands ready to generate when the tidal current is sufficient. The array delivered 4.2 GWh over an 11 month trial, at an array capacity factor of 34 percent and an availability of 93 percent. Wake loss at a downstream spacing of 5 rotor diameters held the downstream output deficit to 9 percent against the front-row value, and the spacing carries the wake result without a thrust penalty on the front row. Capacity factor claims hold for sites with a peak spring current speed above 2.5 m per second; the trial site peak spring current speed was 3.1 m per second. The trial covers a single site and a single array layout, and array behaviour at a second site with a different seabed and a different current profile remains unmeasured. Biofouling control during the trial used diver cleaning on a fixed schedule, and availability under a longer cleaning interval remains unmeasured. The capacity factor claim stands at the scope the trial tested: an array of this layout, at a site of this current class, under the cleaning schedule the trial used. Wider claims wait on a second site and on a longer cleaning interval, and the measurements that would settle both questions are named in the limits above.
